newsitem.title: JORDAN: FEATURE - Jordan's spies come in from the cold -- online.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Jordan's spies come in from the cold -- online.

text.p: Bashar Dahabra's computer business was just starting to take off when the phone call came through.
It was Jordan's feared Mukhabarat intelligence service. They'd had a tip-off, and they wanted to see him straight away.
"They just called me out of the blue and told me to come," said Dahabra, managing director of a firm providing companies with screen pages on the Internet computer web network.
He rushed to the headquarters of Jordan's all-powerful General Intelligence Department (GID) on the outskirts of Amman.
When he got there the GID officer had just one question. Could Dahabra arrange to hook Jordanian intelligence services onto an Internet web-site?

Two months later, on November 11, the GID launched its Internet home page (http://www.arab.net/gid), promising tantalising glimpses into its operation and an e-mail address to anyone who wanted to get in touch.

Dahabra said the project was the first of its kind in the Arab world, where such openness is rare and the image of intelligence services is of a ruthless and invisible Big Brother, terrifying all and accountable to none.
"They wanted to open up channels to the public," he said.
The GID weren't easy clients.
"They were very meticulous. Every comma, every spelling was checked," he said. "We sat down with them for a week to see what we could publish and there were still a lot of no-nos."

The result is a strait-laced guide to Jordan, spiced with a few tidbits about the GID, an organisation with such control over Jordanians' lives they need its clearance to get a passport or take a job in the public sector.
"NEW POLICY OF OPENNESS"
"We have adopted a new policy of openness which we believe will better enhance our ability to serve our people," says a welcoming note from GID director Sameeh al-Buteikhy.
"Naturally, however, due to the nature of our work there exist certain restraints upon the type of information that we will be able to provide through this medium."
Few details are provided but the GID does shed some light on its philosophy.
The department lists 24 Jordanian political parties. Those represented in cabinet it describes as "politically moderate". Others are dismissed as leftist, Islamist, or Arab nationalist.
Close scrutiny of the GID emblem shows an eagle clutching a snake -- the "hidden enemy" which GID is committed to combat.
"Naturally, officers who pass the recruiting stage are those who enjoy a keen sense of patriotism and who are eager to serve their country to the best of their ability," it says.

But the only people named are the seven directors who have run the GID since its founding in 1964. There are no pictures of officials, nor of the GID base, which Jordanians say is a sprawling, ultra-modern complex in west Amman.
Not everyone is impressed by the wave of Jordanian glasnost.

Human rights activist Labib Qamhawi said the GID Internet page was a cheap gimmick. Bassam al-Amoush, an Islamist parliamentary deputy, said he welcomed any opening up by the department but questioned whether it would stop its "intimidation" and detentions of Jordanians.
NATION OF CYBER-SPOOKS
The satirical weekly Abed Rebbo hinted at dark motives.

"An agent in every house!" ran its headline on a story suggesting Jordanians were being turned into a nation of cyber-spooks, informing on their neighbours by Internet. It urged readers to post these questions to the GID:
-- "Will this new service offer the citizen his right to be interrogated and kicked around through the Internet?"
-- "Why do you allow citizens to scream in their cells, but not shout on the streets?"
-- "How many days do you need to get a camel to confess that he is a dinosaur?"
The GID, answering an e-mail query from Reuters, said it had received a "flood of congratulatory messages" since it launched its Internet page.
"It is not our intention to have an open forum for discussion through this medium, but rather to be of service to Jordanians as well as others on a one-to-one basis," it added.
Dahabra said there were 25,000 "visitors" to the GID home page in its first week of operation, five times the amount his other clients get in a month.
He insists the aim was to create a dialogue between the intelligence service and the public, and has no regrets about answering the GID summons a few weeks ago.
"The GID home page has given us new status...I went to a meeting last week with a businessman and the guy wasn't even listening to me -- till he asked me to name some of my clients.
"I told him, the Jordanian General Intelligence Department. Then he started to listen."
